title: The siege of Gurdas Nangal, 1715
hook: starved in a mud fort for months, Banda's men are finally captured

segments.voice: Yesterday, a disguise at Lohgarh and a long hunt through the hills. Your line was keep going. What small step did you take? Today the hunt narrows to one walled place. Go gently with this one. Day eight hundred forty-four.

Mud walls. Not stone, not a fortress on a cliff. A walled compound in a village called Gurdas Nangal, with a ditch around it, and inside, Banda Singh and his people: fighters, and with them families. Outside, an army settles in to wait. Nobody storms the walls. They don't need to. They simply make sure nothing comes in. No grain. No supplies. Tradition says the waiting went on for months. Today: the siege of Gurdas Nangal.
screen: `MUD WALLS AND A DITCH.` → `AN ARMY SETTLES IN TO WAIT.` → `NOTHING COMES IN.`

segments.voice: A siege like this is fought with time and hunger. Sikh tellings describe what happened inside the walls as the food ran out. People ate what grain was left, then the animals, then leaves and grass and the bark of trees. Some tellings go further, and they're hard to hear. They describe people too weak to stand, still keeping their places. Accounts differ on the very end: whether the gate was opened at last, or the army simply walked in on people who could no longer resist. Either way, when hunger had done its work, Banda Singh and the men who were left were taken, worn to almost nothing. The carry is they held on. Not they won. Not they escaped. Sikhs have a word for this: sidak. It means steadfastness, a faith that stays fixed when everything around it gives way. It isn't the same as courage in a charge. Courage can be a single moment. Sidak is a long thing. It's what's left on yet another hungry morning, when nothing heroic is happening and nobody is watching. In Sikh memory, Gurdas Nangal is one of the places where that word was tested hardest. There's a quieter lesson in it too, for a listener whose week has nothing to do with sieges. Much of holding on looks like nothing. It's not leaving. It's getting up again. It's staying where you said you'd stay. That kind of faithfulness doesn't make a good painting, which is maybe why it's worth a word of its own.
screen: `A SIEGE FOUGHT WITH TIME AND HUNGER.` · `GRAIN, THEN LEAVES, THEN BARK.` · `SIDAK: FAITH THAT STAYS FIXED.` · `HOLDING ON OFTEN LOOKS LIKE NOTHING.` · then, large: `THEY HELD ON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of hunger for a minute. Sit, and let the breath settle. Notice your stomach right now: full, empty, somewhere between. Then let your mind rest, gently, on people who are hungry today, near you or far away, who didn't choose it. Don't push for a feeling. Just keep them company in your attention. After a while, come back to the people inside those mud walls, and to the word sidak. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
sidak, steadfastness. The long siege in which Banda Singh and his people were starved in a walled compound at Gurdas Nangal until they were captured. Today's word.
Your line: they held on. Today, give something toward someone's next meal: a donation, a dish for a neighbor, a share of your lunch. Day eight hundred forty-four.

notes: Audit: 'the walls didn't open from inside' overstated the ending; Persian and Mughal accounts describe the starving garrison surrendering or being overrun, so the script now says accounts differ on the very end. The Ardas reference was cut (days 843 and 845 both lean on the Ardas); match pair and trapdoor adjusted.
Editor: dropped 'to their last breath' so the Ardas line no longer repeats day 845's, and softened 'most of holding on' to 'much'.
The title carries a year from the index; the spoken script states no date. 'For months' is from the index hook and told as tradition.
The compound (often called Duni Chand's haveli) is described as walled with a ditch; confirm. Presence of families inside is told in some accounts; confirm.
Details of starvation (animals, leaves, grass, bark) appear in accounts; kept gentle; a Keeper may want less.
